chapters.title: Chapter 1: Real Estate Through an Investor's Eyes

lessons.title: Real Estate vs Equity, Debt and Gold: How Returns Really Compare

children.text: Every family WhatsApp group has one message on repeat: "Property never goes down." Somebody's cousin bought a flat in Thane for ₹20 lakh and "it's worth ₹1 crore now." Somebody else lost money in the stock market in 2008. Case closed. Except it isn't. Those stories compare different periods, ignore rent and costs, skip tax, and forget inflation. This lesson shows you how to compare property with equity, debt and gold properly, so the next time someone makes that claim, you can run the numbers yourself.

body.text: A fair comparison uses the same time period, counts income and growth together, subtracts every cost and tax, and adjusts for inflation. Most property success stories fail all four tests.

children.text: The Four Rules of a Fair Comparison
Same period.
A flat bought in 2003 versus Nifty shares bought at the January 2008 peak is not a comparison. It is cherry-picking.

markDefs.definition: The full return from an investment: income received (rent, dividends, interest) plus the change in its price.

children.text: Total return.
Compare
total return
, not just price. Rent counts for property. Dividends count for equity, which is why the Nifty 50 TRI (Total Return Index) is the right benchmark, not the Nifty 50 price index.
After costs and tax.
Stamp duty, registration, brokerage and maintenance can eat several years of property gains. An index fund on Zerodha Coin costs a fraction of a percent a year.

markDefs.definition: Return after removing the effect of inflation. It measures how much more you can actually buy.

children.text: After inflation.
A 6% return when prices rise 5% a year is a
real return
of about 1%. That is what your purchasing power actually gained.
What the Data Actually Says

body.text: Property is the hardest asset to benchmark. The RBI's House Price Index tracks prices only, not rent, and covers a limited set of cities. It also moved to a new 2022-23 base year in late 2025, which breaks easy long-run comparisons. The Nifty 50 TRI and gold prices, by contrast, have clean daily data going back decades. When someone quotes a precise "real estate return" figure, ask where it came from.

children.text: The Same ₹50 Lakh, Four Ways

Arjun, a 35-year-old in Pune, has ₹50 lakh and a 10-year horizon. Here is what each route could look like using reasonable long-run assumptions. These are illustrations, not forecasts, and all figures are before tax.

cells: ₹46 lakh price plus ₹4 lakh buying costs, 5% appreciation, 2.5% net rent, 1% brokerage on sale

body.title: Value of ₹50 lakh after 10 years (₹ lakh, illustrative)
Show me the math for the flat

children.text: Outlay: ₹46 lakh flat + ₹4 lakh stamp duty, registration, brokerage and legal fees = ₹50 lakh
Price after 10 years at 5%: ₹46 lakh × 1.05^10 = ₹46 lakh × 1.6289 = ₹74.93 lakh
Net rent: 2.5% of ₹46 lakh = ₹1.15 lakh in year one, growing 5% a year with the property's value. Ten years of rent, not reinvested: ₹1.15 lakh × 12.578 = ₹14.46 lakh
Brokerage on sale: 1% of ₹74.93 lakh = ₹0.75 lakh
Total: ₹74.93 lakh + ₹14.46 lakh minus ₹0.75 lakh = ₹88.64 lakh
Annual return: (₹88.64 lakh ÷ ₹50 lakh)^(1/10) minus 1 ≈ 5.9%

body.text: Notice what happened. The flat's price grew 5% a year, but Arjun earned about 5.9% on his ₹50 lakh, less than the FD's 6.5%. Buying costs of ₹4 lakh on day one are a hole the property spends years climbing out of. Change the assumptions and the ranking changes: a hot micro-market growing 9% a year beats the FD easily. The point is not that property always loses. It is that assumptions and costs decide the answer, not family stories.

children.text: Leverage: Why Property Sometimes Looks Unbeatable

Almost nobody buys a flat entirely with cash. Most buyers put down 20% and borrow the rest. That changes the maths completely, in both directions. Take a ₹1 crore flat in Whitefield, Bengaluru: ₹20 lakh down payment, ₹80 lakh home loan at 8%, 2.5% net rental yield. Ignore buying costs and principal repayment to keep it simple.

body.latex: \text{Return on Equity} = \frac{\text{Appreciation} + \text{Net Rent} - \text{Loan Interest}}{\text{Your Down Payment}}
body.caption: Your return is measured on the money you put in, not on the full property price.
One year on a ₹1 crore flat with ₹20 lakh down (illustrative)

body.label: The leverage trap in one line
body.value: A 5% fall in price wiped out 44.5% of the buyer's money
body.context: When the rental yield is below the loan rate, you need strong appreciation just to break even. Leverage turns a mild price dip into a severe loss on your own capital.

body.title: A good year with leverage
body.prompt: Same Whitefield flat: ₹1 crore price, ₹20 lakh down, ₹80 lakh loan at 8%, 2.5% net rent. This time prices rise 8% in the year. What is the return on the buyer's ₹20 lakh, in %?
body.explanation: Appreciation ₹8 lakh + net rent ₹2.5 lakh minus interest ₹6.4 lakh = ₹4.1 lakh. ₹4.1 lakh ÷ ₹20 lakh = 20.5%. Compare that with 5.5% at 5% growth and minus 44.5% at a 5% fall. Leverage makes property returns swing wildly with small changes in price.

body.text: In March 2020, the Nifty 50 fell about 38% from its January high in roughly ten weeks, and everyone saw it. Did Mumbai flat prices fall 38%? Nobody knows, because almost no deals were registered during the lockdown. Stocks show you their risk every second. Property hides it until you try to sell.

children.text: Real Returns: The Number That Matters

body.caption: A quick approximation is nominal return minus inflation.

body.title: Strip out inflation
body.prompt: A flat delivers a 6% total annual return while CPI inflation runs at 5% a year. What is the real return, in %? Use the exact formula and round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (1.06 ÷ 1.05) minus 1 = 0.0095, or about 1.0%. A return that sounds decent in rupees barely grows your purchasing power.

body.title: Name the benchmark
body.textWithBlank: To compare property with Indian equities fairly, you should use the Nifty 50 ___ Return Index, which includes reinvested dividends.
body.explanation: The Total Return Index adds dividends back in. Using the plain price index understates equity returns, just as ignoring rent understates property returns.

body.title: Which comparison is fair?
body.question: Which of these is the fairest way to compare a flat with a Nifty 50 index fund?
options: Flat price growth from 2003 to 2023 vs Nifty 50 price index from 2008 to 2023
Flat price growth only vs Nifty 50 TRI, same period
Flat price growth plus net rent, minus buying and selling costs, vs Nifty 50 TRI minus fund costs, same period
The flat's current portal estimate vs the Nifty 50's best 10-year return
body.explanation: Only option C uses the same period, total return on both sides, and costs on both sides. The others mix periods, ignore rent, or compare an estimate with a best case.

body.title: Rajesh's plot in Lucknow
body.scenario: Rajesh bought a residential plot on the outskirts of Lucknow in 2006 for ₹8 lakh. A local broker says it is now worth ₹48 lakh. At a family dinner he announces that his plot "made 6x" and that his colleague's equity SIPs were a mistake.
body.prompt: Evaluate Rajesh's claim using the four rules of a fair comparison.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Annualise it: (48 ÷ 8)^(1/20) minus 1 ≈ 9.4% a year. That is good, but "6x" sounds far bigger than 9.4%.
2. Compare the same period: ₹8 lakh growing at the Nifty 50 TRI's 12.44% a year for 20 years would be about ₹83 lakh, well above ₹48 lakh.
3. Total return: a vacant plot earns no rent, so 9.4% is the entire return. There may also be 20 years of property tax, boundary wall and upkeep costs to subtract.
4. Costs and tax: stamp duty and registration in 2006, brokerage on sale, and capital gains tax all reduce the true figure.
5. Reliability: ₹48 lakh is a broker's estimate, not a sale price. Until the plot is sold, the gain is unproven, and selling a plot can take months.
6. Real return: with inflation averaging roughly 5% to 6% over the period, the real return is closer to 3% to 4% a year.

body.label: NSE Indices: Nifty 50 Index
body.description: Check official Nifty 50 and Nifty 50 TRI returns and factsheets before comparing any asset with Indian equities.

cards.definition: Income received plus price change. For property: rent plus appreciation.
The Nifty 50 Total Return Index, which includes reinvested dividends. The correct equity benchmark.
The return in rupees, before adjusting for inflation.
The return after inflation: (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) minus 1.
Appreciation plus net rent minus loan interest, divided by your own down payment.
Price risk that exists but is not visible because an asset is not quoted daily, as with physical property.

points: Compare assets over the same period, on total return, after costs and tax, and after inflation.
Use the Nifty 50 TRI for equities, not the price index; include rent for property.
In a cash purchase, buying costs alone can drag a 5% price growth down to a lower return than an FD.
Leverage magnifies property returns both ways: with a 20% down payment, a 5% price fall wiped out 44.5% of the buyer's money in our example.
Property feels safe partly because its price is not quoted daily. The risk is still there.
Convert every "it made 6x" story into an annual, inflation-adjusted return before believing it.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The ₹50 lakh comparison uses illustrative assumptions, not forecasts; actual returns on equity, gold, deposits and property vary widely by period, city and product. Past returns do not guarantee future results. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
